messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Finding transition times
parts:
I'm trying to fit a Stan model to some mechanical creep curves. I attached a sample plot.

The test is a little metal bar is put under a fixed mechanical load and the elongation of that bar is measured vs. time.

For the tests we're concerned with, there are two behaviors in the data. The sample initially creeps non-linearly, and then transitions to linear creep (see attached plot).

The two pieces of data I want from this are the slope of the linear portion of the curve, and an estimate of the time when the creep transitioned from non-linear to linear.

The noise in each sample can be attributed to things like temperature variability, but in our tests it's fairly small. I'm happy just chopping the data set in half and fitting a linear regression to the last bit of data to extract the slope. The difficult thing to characterize is the transition time.

There are ad hoc equations folks use to fit these curves with transition times built in, but they don't actually ever fit the curve well because they don't really fit the non-linear first bit of the curve (and then the fit to the linear part of the curve looks bad).

Does this experiment sound familiar to anything you guys have seen before? I'd like to be able to figure out a reasonable transition time without a model for the first bit of the curve. I think I'm trying to ask the question: "How far back from the end can I go and still be on a line." I'm not sure how to do this. I'm happy doing the slope calculations separately to the transition time ones, if that would make the modeling easier.

Advice? Sorry if I've missed something in the manual.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Finding transition times
parts:
What's the inferential goal here?

If you have a parametric characterization of the initial
part of the curve, then you can fit a traditional change-point
model. There's a description in the first section of the
latent discrete model section; you'd just be using two different
models rather than the same model with different parameters for
before and after the change. Judging from the simulated
data, it looks like it'll be hard to detect that deflection point?

A more general thing to do would be to fit a spline model.
We don't have examples of that, only of the "nonparametric"
Gaussian process models.

Then if you have many measurements for the same load, you
can fit a hierarchical model to find the change point for
that load.

If the initial elongation has some form involving the load,
then using different loads to fit the change point is probably
going to give you the best design. Andrew's written on this
in the context of serial dilution assays, which also have
non-linearities.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Finding transition times
parts:
Hi, my quick thought is that you have to make a decision about whether elongation can be negative.  You seem to have a negative data point but your curve starts at 0.  I don't know the context so I can't answer this for you, but I want to emphasize that this is a modeling choice you must make.
A
